name: Dry Mead
overallimpression: A classic, unflavored mead with no residual sugar sweetness, highlighting the pure varietal character of the fermented honey with clean alcohol and refreshing acidity.
aroma: Honey aroma may be subtle, although should not be completely absent. The varietal character of the floral source is noticeable. Clean fermentation profile with no diacetyl, fusel alcohols, or heavy sulfur. Mild floral and fruit notes are common.
appearance: Color may range from water-white to deep amber depending on the honey varietal used. Brilliant clarity is expected, with no haze. Still, pétillant, or sparkling carbonation stand.
flavor: Bone dry to dry finish without sweetness. Pure varietal honey flavor with supporting acidity, moderate alcohol warmth, and a clean, refreshing lingering finish. Tannins may provide subtle structure.
mouthfeel: Light to medium body depending on strength. Smooth with pleasant alcohol warmth. Carbonation ranges from still (no carbonation) to sparkling (champagne-like effervescence).
comments: Traditional meads feature honey without fruit, spices, or flavorings. Balance between acidity, alcohol, and honey varietal profile is essential.
history: Traditional mead has ancient origins across Europe, Africa, and Asia, celebrated in mythology and historical texts as the nectar of the gods.
characteristicingredients: Monofloral or wildflower honey (clover, orange blossom, tupelo, wildflower), water, yeast nutrient, clean wine or mead yeast.
stylecomparison: Similar in balance to a dry white wine or crisp cider, but distinguished by varietal honey aromatics.
commercialexamples: B. Nektar Continental, Schramm's Statement Dry, Moonlight Meadery Desire Dry

name: Semi-Sweet Mead
overallimpression: A balanced traditional mead with noticeable honey sweetness that is harmoniously countered by natural acidity and clean alcohol, offering rich floral honey character without cloying heaviness.
aroma: Prominent, pleasant honey aromatics showcasing the varietal characteristics of the honey. Clean alcohol presentation with subtle floral, fruity, or waxy nuances. No off-fermentation traits.
appearance: Pale straw to deep gold or amber. Crystal clear with excellent clarity. Viscosity and legs may be visible on higher-strength examples.
flavor: Moderate honey sweetness balanced by supportive acidity. Varietal honey flavors (citrus blossom, herbal, earthy, berry-like) are rich and evident. Pleasant, round finish with balanced sweetness.
mouthfeel: Medium body with a pleasing, silky mouth-coating character. Smooth warmth from alcohol. Carbonation can be still, pétillant, or sparkling.
comments: The most popular style of traditional mead. Requires excellent balance between residual sugar and natural honey acidity.
history: Classical honey wine style popular throughout medieval and Renaissance Europe.
characteristicingredients: High-quality varietal honey, pure water, yeast nutrients, clean fermenting wine or mead yeast strains.
stylecomparison: Comparable to an off-dry or semi-sweet German Riesling, but with luscious honey varietal presence.
commercialexamples: Redstone Traditional Mountain Honey Wine, Medovina Autumn Harvest, B. Nektar Wildflower Semi-Sweet

name: Sweet Mead
overallimpression: A rich, full-bodied, dessert-style traditional mead with pronounced honey sweetness, unctuous mouthfeel, and deep floral honey intensity balanced by acidity and warming alcohol.
aroma: Intense, rich honey aromatics reminiscent of raw honeycomb, nectar, and blossoms. Clean fermentation with noticeable alcohol warmth.
appearance: Deep gold to rich coppery amber. Brilliant clarity. Pronounced legs and viscosity coat the glass when swirled.
flavor: Rich, luscious honey sweetness that lingers on the palate. Acidity and alcohol prevent it from being cloying. Long, honey-saturated finish with subtle floral and caramel complexities.
mouthfeel: Full, viscous body with luxurious silkiness. Warm alcohol finish. Often presented still, though pétillant or sparkling versions can provide wonderful contrast.
comments: Often served as an after-dinner dessert beverage or digestif. Excellent aging potential over multiple years.
history: Celebrated in Nordic and Slavic traditions as a feast and celebratory beverage.
characteristicingredients: Concentrated high-gravity honey must, yeast nutrients, alcohol-tolerant wine or mead yeast.
stylecomparison: Similar to a French Sauternes or late-harvest dessert wine in richness and balance.
commercialexamples: Schramm's Heritage, Kuhnhenn Bourbon Barrel French Toast, White Winter Sweet Mead

name: Cyser
overallimpression: A harmonious blend of fermented honey and apple juice (cider), uniting crisp orchard apple character and varietal honey notes with balanced acidity and sweetness.
aroma: Delightful fusion of fresh or baked apple aromatics with varietal honey notes. Subtle malic acidity is noticeable, creating a bright bouquet. Clean fermentation profile.
appearance: Pale straw to deep gold. Clear to brilliant clarity. A persistent mousse or rim of bubbles in sparkling examples.
flavor: Both apple and honey flavors are clearly discernible, interacting seamlessly. Malic acidity from the apples cuts through honey sweetness, providing a refreshing, vinous finish.
mouthfeel: Light to medium-full body. Crisp acidity gives a refreshing bite. Sparkling versions enhance the crisp fruitiness.
comments: Made by fermenting honey mixed with fresh-pressed apple cider or juice instead of water.
history: Cyser has an extensive history in England, France (Normandy), and colonial North America where apple orchards were abundant.
characteristicingredients: Fresh unpasteurized cider apple juice, mild floral honey, wine or cider yeast.
stylecomparison: Crisper than a traditional mead; richer and more complexly aromatic than a standard hard cider.
commercialexamples: Schramm's The Statement Cyser, Moonlight Meadery Kurt's Apple Pie, B. Nektar Zombie Killer

name: Pyment
overallimpression: A marriage of honey and wine grapes, capturing the vinous depth and tannins of grape must alongside luscious honey varietal nuances.
aroma: Aromatics combine distinct grape wine characteristics (red or white wine varietal notes) with floral, waxy honey notes. Vinous, clean, and expressive.
appearance: Varies by grape type: white pyments range from straw to golden; red pyments range from ruby red to deep purple. Excellent clarity.
flavor: Complex balance of wine grape fruitiness, grape acidity/tannin, and honey sweetness and flavor. Neither grape nor honey should dominate to the exclusion of the other.
mouthfeel: Medium to full body. Grape tannins may contribute pleasant astringency and structure, especially in red grape varieties.
comments: Can be crafted using red wine grapes (Cabernet, Pinot Noir, Syrah) or white wine grapes (Chardonnay, Riesling, Muscat).
history: Pyment was widely consumed throughout antiquity in ancient Greece and Rome, and celebrated across medieval Europe as Hippocras or Clarre when spiced.
characteristicingredients: Wine grape must or juice, varietal honey, wine yeast strains.
stylecomparison: Bridges the gap between fine varietal wine and mead, exhibiting vinous structure with honey complexity.
commercialexamples: Redstone Pinot Noir Pyment, Moonlight Meadery Razz What She Said, Schramm's Black Agnes

name: Berry Mead
overallimpression: A luscious fruit mead made with berries (raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, strawberries, currants), featuring vibrant berry fruitiness and vivid color balanced by honey sweetness and acidity.
aroma: Intense berry aroma showcasing natural fruit character (tart raspberry, jammy blackberry, earthy blueberry). Supporting floral honey notes.
appearance: Vibrant colors ranging from ruby pink to deep purple, garnet, or blue-violet. Brilliant clarity.
flavor: Bursting with real berry flavor, balancing tart fruit acidity with residual honey sweetness. Berry seeds may lend a subtle, pleasing tannic structure.
mouthfeel: Medium-light to full body depending on sweetness and berry variety. Berry acidity provides a clean, refreshing palate lift.
comments: Single berry varietals or multi-berry blends (e.g. four-berry melomels) are both common.
history: Traditional Nordic, Baltic, and North American meadmaking traditions using forest and garden berries.
characteristicingredients: Whole fresh or frozen berries, honey, pectic enzyme, wine yeast.
stylecomparison: More tart and deeply colored than traditional mead or cyser; intensely fruit-forward.
commercialexamples: Schramm's The Heart of Darkness, Superstition Marion, Moonlight Meadery Desire

name: Stone Fruit Mead
overallimpression: A luscious fruit mead crafted with stone fruits (cherries, peaches, apricots, plums, nectarines), featuring aromatic stone fruit character and gentle almond-like stone nuances harmonized with honey.
aroma: Expressive stone fruit bouquet—tart pie cherry, juicy peach, delicate apricot, or rich plum—with fragrant floral honey aromatics.
appearance: Pale amber (peach/apricot) to deep ruby red (cherry/plum). Excellent clarity.
flavor: Rich stone fruit flavor with characteristic fruit tartness balancing honey sweetness. In cherry meads (kieska), sour cherry acidity provides remarkable balance.
mouthfeel: Smooth and velvety. Medium body. Stone fruit acidity keeps the finish vibrant.
comments: Cherry mead is historically known as Cherry Melomel or Krupnik/Kieska. Pit contact can lend subtle marzipan or almond complexity.
history: Deep roots across Poland, Germany, and Eastern Europe where sour cherries and plums were widely grown and fermented.
characteristicingredients: Sour cherries (Montmorency), sweet cherries, peaches, apricots, plums, floral honey, wine yeast.
stylecomparison: Richer than berry mead with distinct stone fruit fleshiness and subtle pit tannin.
commercialexamples: Schramm's The Statement Balaton, Superstition Flora, Kuhnhenn Cherry Melomel

name: Melomel
overallimpression: A fruit mead made with any other fruit not covered in categories M2A–M2D (such as mango, passionfruit, citrus, melon, rhubarb, or mixed fruit blends), expressing the essence of the fruit balanced with honey.
aroma: Distinct fruit aroma reflective of the featured fruits, blended seamlessly with honey sweetness and floral notes.
appearance: Color varies with fruit choice, from golden yellow (citrus/mango) to deep crimson. Clear to brilliant.
flavor: The fruit should be readily identifiable on the palate and in balance with the honey. Natural fruit acidity provides structure and freshness.
mouthfeel: Body varies with fruit pectin, tannins, and sweetness level. Pleasant alcohol warmth.
comments: Catch-all category for tropical fruits, citrus, pome fruits other than apples, and creative multi-fruit combinations.
history: Melomel is the historical umbrella term for all fruit meads dating back to classical antiquity.
characteristicingredients: Tropical fruit, citrus, melon, rhubarb, or multi-fruit blends, varietal honey, wine yeast.
stylecomparison: Defined by the specific fruit variety used, balanced by sweet honey foundation.
commercialexamples: B. Nektar The Dude's Rug, Superstition Dune Dwellers, Moonlight Meadery Jazz

name: Fruit and Spice Mead
overallimpression: A mead featuring a seamless combination of both fruit and spices, herbs, or botanicals, creating an intricate sensory synergy where fruit, spice, and honey elevate one another.
aroma: Complex aromatics combining fruit character and aromatic spices with floral honey. Spices should complement rather than overwhelm the fruit.
appearance: Color is determined by the fruit choice. Spices should not create persistent haze.
flavor: Layered flavor profile: fruit acidity and flavors marry with warming or herbal spice notes, backed by honey sweetness and clean alcohol.
mouthfeel: Medium to full body. Spices (like cinnamon or ginger) may impart a pleasant warming sensation on the finish.
comments: Examples include apple-cinnamon mead, blackberry-sage mead, and cherry-vanilla mead.
history: Spiced fruit meads have historical roots in spiced mulled wines and medieval holiday banquets.
characteristicingredients: Fruit, whole culinary spices (cinnamon, clove, vanilla, ginger), honey, wine yeast.
stylecomparison: More complex than a pure fruit mead or pure spiced mead; balance between all three elements is paramount.
commercialexamples: B. Nektar Kill All The Golfers, Superstition Peanut Butter Jelly Crime, Schramm's Nutmeg Melomel

name: Spice, Herb or Vegetable Mead
overallimpression: Also known historically as Metheglin, this mead incorporates culinary spices, herbs, botanicals, peppers, or vegetables into honey, creating a savory, warming, or refreshing spiced elixir.
aroma: Expressive spice or herbal aroma—such as ginger, cinnamon, clove, rosemary, lavender, vanilla, or hot peppers—in balance with honey aromatics.
appearance: Light straw to deep amber. Some spices may tint the color slightly. Clarity is typically brilliant.
flavor: The spice or herb character should be distinct and pleasant, harmonizing with the natural sweetness of honey without harsh vegetal or medicinal astringency.
mouthfeel: Body varies with sweetness. Spices like capsaicin or ginger add pleasant heat or tingling carbonation.
comments: The historical Welsh word 'Metheglin' comes from 'meddyg' (physician) and 'llyn' (liquor), reflecting its traditional medicinal and herbal roots.
history: One of the oldest documented spiced beverages, Metheglin was popular in ancient Wales, England, and medieval monastic medicine.
characteristicingredients: Culinary herbs, spices, hot peppers, coffee, tea, chocolate, or vegetables, varietal honey, wine yeast.
stylecomparison: Distinguished by herbal/spice additions without fruit; sweeter versions showcase vanilla and warming holiday spices.
commercialexamples: B. Nektar Necromangocon, Moonlight Meadery Smitten, Kuhnhenn Vanilla Metheglin

name: Braggot
overallimpression: A hybrid beverage made by fermenting both honey and malted barley or wheat, incorporating hops for bitterness and aroma, fusing the malt richness of beer with the floral sweetness of mead.
aroma: A harmonious blend of malt aromatics (bready, biscuity, roasty, or caramel notes) and floral honey aromatics. Hop aroma can range from low to moderate with floral, herbal, or citrus notes.
appearance: Straw to dark brown depending on malt grist used. Clear to hazy. Unlike pure mead, braggot typically forms a persistent foamy beer-like head.
flavor: Rich malt flavors (bready, caramel, toasty) merge with sweet varietal honey notes. Hop bitterness is present to balance both malt and honey sweetness.
mouthfeel: Medium-full to full body with a smooth, velvety mouthfeel. Moderate to high carbonation creates beer-like foam.
comments: Must have a noticeable character of both beer (malt and hops) and mead (honey). Neither component should be completely masked.
history: Braggot has Celtic origins and was mentioned in Chaucer's Canterbury Tales in the 14th century.
characteristicingredients: Malted barley (base malt, caramel malt, roasted malt), brewing hops, wildflower honey, beer or mead yeast.
stylecomparison: Crosses the boundary between craft beer (like a barleywine, scotch ale, or Belgian dubbel) and strong honey mead.
commercialexamples: White Winter Black Bear Braggot, Kuhnhenn Braggot, Brotherton Braggot

name: Historical Mead
overallimpression: A mead style based on historical recipes or traditional regional honey drinks (such as Polish Dwójniak or Trójniak, Medovukha, Omphacomel, or Rhodomel) that do not fit standard categories.
aroma: Reflective of historical ingredients and processing, which may include wild yeast, souring microflora, oak aging, or traditional herbal blends.
appearance: Varies by historical style; from pale straw to deep amber. Clarity can range from hazy farmhouse to brilliant.
flavor: Unique historical balance, which might incorporate light smoke, herbal bitterness, wild sourness, or intense residual honey sweetness.
mouthfeel: Varies with historical guidelines, ranging from light farmhouse quenchers to viscous dessert nectars.
comments: Entrants must specify the historical source or traditional reference for the entry.
history: Celebrates ancient meadmaking traditions from Poland (Miód Pitny), Russia (Medovukha), and ancient Rome.
characteristicingredients: Traditional regional honeys, ancient herbs, birch sap, wild yeasts, wood barrels.
stylecomparison: Distinct from modern clean meads, often showing rustic, wood-aged, or historic character.
commercialexamples: Apis Poltorak Polish Mead, Apis Dwojniak, Medovukha Farmhouse Meads

name: Experimental Mead
overallimpression: An innovative mead that pushes boundaries using unconventional ingredients, novel fermentation techniques, non-standard barrels, or multiple specialty processes that do not fit into any other category.
aroma: Intriguing and creative bouquet showcasing experimental ingredients (spirit barrels, kombucha cultures, smoke, savory ingredients) alongside honey.
appearance: Varies widely based on experimental ingredients.
flavor: Creative harmony between unexpected ingredients and honey. Innovation should produce an enjoyable, cohesive beverage.
mouthfeel: Varies with process; may feature carbonation sensations, barrel wood tannins, or creamy textures.
comments: Showcases the cutting edge of contemporary meadcraft and artisanal experimentation.
history: Modern craft meadery movement pushing the frontiers of fermentation.
characteristicingredients: Any creative fermentable, spirit barrel aging, unusual botanicals, honey, novel yeast/bacteria.
stylecomparison: Individualistic by design, evaluated on creativity and sensory balance.
commercialexamples: Superstition Tahitian Honeymoon, B. Nektar Dwarf Invasion, Moonlight Meadery Kurt's Fantasy
